nameStory: The alkali buttercup gets its name from its ability to thrive in alkaline, salty soils where most other buttercups can't survive. It's also called seaside buttercup because it often grows near coastlines and salt marshes, cheerfully blooming in conditions that would stress out its inland cousins. The 'buttercup' part comes from the family's characteristic shiny yellow petals that look like they've been polished with butter.
description: Alkali buttercup is a low-growing perennial wildflower that spreads along the ground with creeping stems called stolons. Unlike the tall, upright buttercups you might know, this one stays close to the earth, rarely getting taller than 15 inches. It produces small, pale yellow flowers with 5-8 petals that are quite modest compared to other buttercups. The plant sends out runners that root wherever they touch moist soil, creating small colonies in wet, salty places.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pale yellow flowers with 5-8 petals, each petal less than half an inch long, much paler and smaller than typical bright golden buttercups

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Prostrate creeping stems that root at nodes, forming low mats rather than standing upright like most buttercups

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Variable kidney-shaped to rounded leaves on long stalks at the base, with notched or slightly divided edges that feel smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Central flower part becomes a distinctive cylindrical cluster of small dry fruits that protrudes noticeably from the flower center

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Found exclusively in wet, alkaline or salty soils like salt marshes and alkaline springs where other buttercups won't grow

habitat: In New England, alkali buttercup is found in coastal salt marshes, alkaline wetlands, and areas with mineral-rich spring seepage. It thrives in places where the soil stays consistently moist and has higher salt or mineral content than typical garden soil. Look for it near the coast in brackish areas or inland at natural springs and mineral seeps.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge early, forming low rosettes of kidney-shaped leaves on long stalks. The creeping stems begin to spread and root in suitable moist spots.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with small pale yellow flowers appearing on short stalks above the foliage. The distinctive cylindrical seed heads begin forming after flowers fade.
seasonality.fall: Mature seed heads are prominent while leaves may begin to yellow. Plants continue to spread via runners if conditions remain moist.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level in harsh cold, but established root systems and stolons survive to regrow next year.

funFact: This tough little buttercup is like the plant world's extreme athlete - it actually prefers salty, alkaline soil conditions that would kill most other wildflowers, making it one of the few buttercups that can handle beachside living!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small yellow wildflowers in wet areas, but the combination of very pale yellow flowers, creeping growth habit, and salty/alkaline habitat is distinctive. Regular buttercups have much brighter golden flowers and prefer fresh water, not salt water conditions.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a buttercup, this species was recently moved to its own genus (Halerpestes) based on genetic studies, though it's still in the buttercup family. Many field guides may still list it under the old genus name Ranunculus, so don't be confused if you see it called Ranunculus cymbalarius.
compareHints: Alkali buttercup is the only species in its genus found in New England, making it unique among our buttercups. Compared to common buttercups in the Ranunculus genus, it has much paler flowers, a distinctly creeping growth habit, and tolerance for salty conditions. While other buttercups prefer rich, moist but fresh soils, this species specifically seeks out alkaline and saline environments that would stress its relatives.
